text.p: Australia, trailing some of its Third World neighbours in protecting babies from killer diseases, unveiled an ambitious plan on Tuesday to nearly double immunisation levels.

Health Minister Michael Wooldridge announced a mixture of cash payments, publicity programmes and controls to encourage parents to immunise their young children against potentially fatal diseases such as measles, whooping cough and tetanus.

"Australian children are dying of utterly preventable illnesses and I have no intention of going down in history as the health minister who sat on his hands while children are dying unnecessarily -- this will fix it," Wooldridge told reporters.
Barely half Australia's children under six are immunised -- one of the worst rates in the developed world and lagging well behind countries such as China and Indonesia.
Wooldridge, a medical doctor, has warned one in 4,000 children would die each year unless the immunisation rate rises to more than 95 percent.
He earlier told parliament doctors would be offered cash rewards for high immunisation rates among their patients and some government payments to families would be tied to immunisation.
Parents will also have to present proof of immunisation for their children to be allowed into childcare centres and schools.
But immunisation will not be compulsory and parents who strongly object, or whose children could not be immunised for medical reasons could gain an exemption, Wooldridge said.
